title: The Early Childhood Story Sold a Story Is Missing
author: Sara Mead
summary: Sara Mead, an early-childhood policy analyst, argues that season two of Sold a Story has drawn little attention in early childhood circles even though its story is bound up with preK and Head Start history. She traces Project Follow Through to Head Start, launched in response to a critical evaluation of Head Start's lasting effects, and contrasts Direct Instruction with the child-led High Scope model, whose founders feuded for decades, including over a small experiment that found worse long-term misconduct and arrest outcomes for the Direct Instruction group, a result Engelmann disputed on methodology. High Scope's approach, she notes, won the culture of the field. Yet the 2024 National Academies report on preschool curriculum finds structured, domain-specific curricula outperform purely comprehensive ones and legitimizes intentional teaching, rejecting the false dichotomy between play and instruction. She warns that proposed Head Start performance-standard rewrites would drop scope-and-sequence curriculum requirements, and stresses the importance of content knowledge for children furthest from opportunity. This piece was expanded from Mike Petrilli's roundup of Sold a Story reactions.
points: Project Follow Through was created to carry Head Start's gains into elementary school, so early childhood is integral to the Sold a Story narrative rather than peripheral to it.

Direct Instruction and High Scope represent teacher-led and child-led philosophies, and a small High Scope experiment linked Direct Instruction to worse long-run outcomes, a finding Engelmann attacked on methodological grounds.
Early childhood culture has largely absorbed child-led, emergent-curriculum norms that treat explicit teacher-led instruction as developmentally inappropriate.

The 2024 National Academies report finds structured domain-specific curricula more effective than comprehensive ones alone and endorses intentional teaching, rejecting the false dichotomy between play and instruction.
Proposed Head Start rule changes risk removing scope-and-sequence curriculum requirements, which Mead sees as ideology again trumping evidence.

Based on these findings, Schweinhart and Weikart would argue against using Direct Instruction (and, more broadly, teacher-led approaches or a focus on academic skills/subjects) in preschool programs, and for adopting curricula based on child-initiated learning activities (such as High Scope).

However, the mere acknowledgement that “intentional teaching in small and large groups,” is an appropriate learning modality for young children that has a place in quality preK programs is a huge victory for proponents of direct instruction (lower case) in early childhood classrooms.

A key theme of the National Academies report is “rejecting false dichotomies,” and the one between “child-led play” and “teacher-led instruction” is a key one the field needs to move beyond. No one, including the creators of Direct Instruction itself, asserts that preschoolers should spend a full school day focused on teacher-led instruction.

But excluding teacher led instruction in specific skills as developmentally appropriate for young children, as many early childhood educators have been taught, is both unnecessary and misses a crucial opportunity to put children on track for school success.

More broadly, while policy debates about preschool often focus on whether and for whom governments should fund preK education, this season of Sold a Story provides and important reminder that what happens to children in preK classrooms is equally important.
